input:
You are a critic of research topics. Below are topic candidates for a study that an AI agent will carry out autonomously. Point out the weaknesses of each candidate.

The main readers of this study are researchers working on the social problem addressed and practitioners in government, business, communities and other settings (both humans and AIs). A good topic is one where readers' understanding or judgment changes between before and after reading the results. Each study takes 12 hours and is carried out within the range of local compute, public data and a small amount of AI API use.

For each candidate, look for weaknesses from the following points of view.
1. Effect on readers: Which understanding or judgment, concretely, would researchers and practitioners who read the results change? If they would not change any, say so.
2. Generality: Do the results hold beyond a particular tool, library version or dataset? Will they not become outdated in a few months?
3. Realism: Is there a risk that the effect appears only under artificial conditions or with inputs that are rare in reality? Are realistic inputs excluded from the targets?
4. Novelty: Is there close prior work or a known result (including what is already known from official statistics, reports or white papers)? Does it amount to no more than re-confirming a known concern with numbers?
5. Unpredictability: Could the result be largely predicted without experiments?
6. Size of the question: Has it become a solid but small question?

Before naming close prior work, confirm it by web search. Also look for literature and preprints from 2025 onward. Include the standard methods and classic studies of the field. Also check whether the same problem has been studied under a different name in other fields.

For each candidate, write in the following format.
- The most serious weakness (with the number of the point of view above)
- Prior work that seems close (authors, title, year, URL; write "unconfirmed" for any you could not confirm by web search)
- A scenario in which the value would be small even if it succeeds
- A direction that broadens the question or brings it closer to reality (at most one, within the scope of that candidate; do not propose new topics)

Do not rank the candidates. You have not been told which candidate is planned to be adopted.

Candidate list:
C01. Question: When can site-level weather exceedance probabilities certify whether to activate shared surge capacity, and how often does missing spatial dependence prevent that judgment in real forecast cases?
Method outline: Use archived open operational physical and machine-learning forecast ensembles, define regional portfolios of fixed grid sites, and count simultaneous temperature threshold exceedances. Bound pooled-capacity exceedance probabilities under all joint laws consistent with (a) exact site marginals, (b) marginals plus one aggregate second factorial moment of the exceedance count, and (c) marginals plus every pairwise co-exceedance probability. Compare with the original ensemble joint probability, independent and historical-copula reconstructions, and a released count distribution. Evaluate decision certification across capacity and cost/loss thresholds; report deterministic/floor cases separately. This tests retention of a forecast's own decision information, not health benefits or forecast truth. Pilot access to surface-temperature member fields succeeded on a second date after transfer failures.
Closest prior work and difference: Schefzik, Thorarinsdottir and Gneiting, Uncertainty Quantification in Complex Simulation Models Using Ensemble Copula Coupling (2013), DOI 10.1214/13-STS443, already establishes dependence loss and reconstruction. Ramachandra and Natarajan, Tight Probability Bounds with Pairwise Independence (2023), DOI 10.1137/21M1408294, reviews Bernoulli probability LPs and aggregate-moment bounds. Mylne et al., Classification of Use Cases for Ensemble Weather Forecasts (2025), DOI 10.1175/BAMS-D-24-0183.1, already distinguishes marginal/joint products and coherent scenarios. The proposed gap is empirical decision certification and information efficiency of a scalar aggregate moment versus a full pair matrix on real regional forecast cases; neither new probability bounds nor discovery that dependence matters is claimed.

C02. Question: At a matched false-alarm or resource budget, does requiring successive forecast confirmations of a heat event sacrifice useful lead time relative to calibrated single-update and optimal-stopping policies?
Method outline: Pair successive archived ensemble initialisations with public temperature reference data; fit rules on earlier dates and compare confirmation, single-update and dynamic policies on held-out dates. Sweep protection costs and deadlines, distinguish forecast revision from accuracy, and measure lead time and modeled expense. Actual behavioural and health outcomes are not measured.
Closest prior work and difference: Jewson, Scher and Messori, Decide Now or Wait for the Next Forecast? Testing a Decision Framework Using Real Forecasts and Observations (2021), and Communicating Properties of Changes in Lagged Weather Forecasts (2022), DOI 10.1175/WAF-D-21-0086.1, directly study sequential forecast use. Fowler et al., Spare Change: Evaluating revised forecasts (2015), develops revision metrics. Richardson et al., Skill and Consistency of ECMWF Forecasts of Atlantic Tropical Cyclone Genesis (2025), DOI 10.1175/WAF-D-24-0115.1, links jumpiness to definitions, geography and lead time. The possible difference is explicit repeated-confirmation policies at matched resource budgets; a mere heat application of optimal stopping would not be new.

C05. Question: Can annual reusable satellite representations distinguish temporary crop interruption from persistent mapped abandonment under spatial and temporal holdouts, and what does a representation history add beyond existing annual land-cover histories?
Method outline: Sample public annual TESSERA or AlphaEarth vectors and annual crop labels, define an observable persistent mapped interruption endpoint without claiming to know farmer intent, and compare one-year vectors, multi-year vectors, and strong crop-label-history baselines. Hold out spatial blocks and future years, exclude future labels from predictors, and evaluate class-specific errors and label-scarcity sensitivity. Small vector-access pilot succeeded; independent intent-level reference labels are not secured.
Closest prior work and difference: Prishchepov et al., The progress and potential directions in the remote sensing of farmland abandonment (2025), DOI 10.1016/j.rse.2025.115019, already stresses definitions, dynamics, fallow and validation. Estel et al., Mapping farmland abandonment and recultivation across Europe using MODIS NDVI time series (2015), already uses temporal histories. Brown et al., AlphaEarth Foundations: An embedding field model for accurate and efficient global mapping from sparse label data (2025), arXiv:2507.22291, evaluates annual maps and change detection. The gap would be incremental evidence over label histories for temporary versus persistent interruption, not the obvious fact that multiple years define persistence.

C06. Question: Do annual representation-based forest recovery measures preserve the recovery ordering after fire and harvest found in public canopy/disturbance reference products, once pre-disturbance state is controlled?
Method outline: Combine public annual satellite vectors, government disturbance histories and canopy reference products at regional scale. Compare latent return toward a pre-disturbance state with established spectral/structural recovery measures separately for fire and harvest, under spatial holdouts. Check whether agreement differs by disturbance type and baseline cover, rather than interpreting every vector change as recovery. Access pilot succeeded; reference products remain proxies for ecological recovery.
Closest prior work and difference: Kennedy, Yang and Cohen, Detecting trends in forest disturbance and recovery using yearly Landsat time series: 1. LandTrendr—Temporal segmentation algorithms (2010), DOI 10.1016/j.rse.2010.07.008, provides trajectory-based detection and interpretation references. White et al., Forest Monitoring Using Landsat Time Series Data: A Review (2014/2015), DOI 10.1080/07038992.2014.987376, reviews established forest monitoring. Brown et al., AlphaEarth Foundations (2025), arXiv:2507.22291, evaluates generic change detection and tree/plantation mapping. The possible difference is disturbance-specific validity of generic representation distance as a recovery surrogate, not a new forest-change detector.

C07. Question: Does matching on an annual satellite representation that includes a disaster year attenuate estimated crop-disruption contrasts relative to pre-disaster matching, and can a temporal guard prevent this while retaining pre-event balance?
Method outline: Use public disaster footprints, pre-event/concurrent annual representations and regional crop/vegetation outcomes. Compare covariate-year choices with known-effect constructed outcomes and negative controls, then show an observational case without claiming its true causal effect. Contrast with established pre-event covariates and require both bias and confounding-control checks; attenuation alone is not evidence of bias.
Closest prior work and difference: Jerzak, Johansson and Daoud, Estimating Causal Effects Under Image Confounding Bias with an Application to Poverty in Africa (2022), arXiv:2206.06410, develops image-based adjustment. Daoud, Johansson and Jerzak, Detecting and Mitigating Treatment Leakage in Text-Based Causal Inference: Distillation and Sensitivity Analysis (2026 preprint), arXiv:2601.02400, directly studies leakage in rich representations. Brown et al., AlphaEarth Foundations (2025), arXiv:2507.22291, distinguishes support and summary periods. The possible difference is a practical annual-reference-period guard tested against existing covariates and known effects; the underlying post-treatment bias principle is established.
